opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd give myself a passing grade, but there's still a lot of room to improve.

When I started Meshy, I was a researcher and an engineer at heart. My comfort zone was writing compilers and graphics code, like Taichi. Becoming a CEO meant learning a completely different set of skills: hiring, fundraising, talking to customers, setting strategy, and sometimes making decisions with very incomplete information. None of that came naturally to me.

I think I've done reasonably well on the product and technical vision side. We moved fast, we bet early on AI-generated 3D, and we built something people actually use and pay for. That gives me some confidence that the direction was right.

Where I've had to grow the most is on the people side. As an engineer, you can debug a program, and it behaves deterministically. Organizations don't work like that. I've made mistakes in hiring, in communication, in how quickly I delegated things. Early on I wanted to be involved in everything, and that doesn't scale. Learning to trust the team and focus on the few decisions that really matter has been a big lesson.

So my self-assessment is: I'm a much better CEO than I was two years ago, but I'm still learning every day. I try to treat it like research. Form a hypothesis, try something, look at the results, and iterate. The job keeps changing as the company grows, so I have to keep changing too.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly? I'd give myself a passing grade, maybe a B, with a lot of room to grow.

The thing I keep coming back to is that I didn't start out as a CEO. I started out as a researcher. I spent years at MIT building Taichi, writing compilers, caring about things like how fast a simulation runs on a GPU. That kind of work has a very clear feedback loop: the code either works or it doesn't, the benchmark either improves or it doesn't. Running a company is nothing like that. The feedback is noisy, delayed, and often contradictory.

Where I think I've done reasonably well is on the technical vision. We bet early that generative AI would reshape 3D content creation, back when most people thought 3D was too hard, too sparse in data, too niche. We stayed focused on the actual pain points of game developers and artists instead of chasing whatever was trendy that month. And we shipped. We iterated fast, listened to users, and kept improving the quality of the models. I'm proud of the team for that.

Where I've had to learn the most is on the people side. Hiring the right people, letting go of control, communicating clearly when things are ambiguous. Early on I probably tried to be involved in too many details, because that's what a researcher instinctively does. I had to learn that my job is to make the team effective, not to be the smartest person in every room. I also underestimated how much of the job is just repetition: saying the same vision over and over until it actually sinks in, for the team, for investors, for users.

And there have been real mistakes. Timing on certain products, prioritization calls where we spent months on something that didn't matter as much as we thought. I try to be honest with the team about those, because I'd rather we build a culture where mistakes are acknowledged quickly than one where everyone pretends to be perfect.

So, not a perfect CEO. But I think I'm a much better one than I was two years ago, and the goal is to keep that slope steep. If I'm not noticeably better a year from now, that would be the real failure.

astra-6.text: I think I’m still learning. My background is technical, so I’m more comfortable thinking about research and building products. So I’d say there’s plenty of room for improvement. The real measure is whether we’re building something people value and whether the team can keep getting better.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’m still learning. My background is technical, so I’m most comfortable building things and solving engineering problems. As CEO, I have to think much more about the team: Are we working on the right problems? Does everyone understand the priorities? Am I giving people enough context and room to make decisions?

I’m proud of what we’re building at Meshy, but I wouldn’t give myself a final score. The real measure is whether our users find the product useful and whether the team can keep getting better. My job is to help make both of those happen.
